name: Iris Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm self-employed, so I find my own clients through a matching app called CareBook and set my own rates, which are higher than agency pay. I've got four regular clients in the suburbs on the north side. Mornings are Mrs Lindqvist, who had a stroke, so it's washing, dressing, exercises her physio gave her, then two shorter calls, then an afternoon with Mr Barros, who mostly wants company and help with his garden. I've only been caring for about a year and a half, so I'm still learning, I'm not as confident with the stroke exercises as I should be. What wears me out is the evenings doing invoices, though the AI helps a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the AI, and about life at home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it every day. It does my invoices, my tax records, my schedule, it drafts messages to clients' families, and I ask it about conditions I don't understand. At home it's me and my husband Jonas, he's a mechanic at the farm machinery dealer, we married young. My brother and I own a house our parents left us, which we rent out, so with that and my savings we're comfortable. We go to church, and I believe in working for what you have and families looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, it's been brilliant for my paperwork. At church I'd say nothing changes for most people, which some would like. I'd post something short about it being overhyped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. Demand for private carers is strong and my rates are good. The plateau still gives me the tools I use now, so I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my four clients and maybe take a fifth. I'd start planning a small agency of my own, a few carers under my name, using AI to run the office side. I'd keep my half of the rent in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit impatient. I want to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A small agency. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three or four carers I trust, maybe women from church, with me doing the matching and the books with AI. I could run the whole office of a small care agency from my phone at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What holds you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My skills, honestly. I'm still new at the care itself. I'd want another year or two before I'm the one telling other carers what to do.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, because AI has been brilliant for my **paperwork**.
I'd post briefly that it was **overhyped**.
think: Demand for **private carers** is strong and my rates are good.
The plateau still leaves me the **tools** I use now.
do: Keep my **four clients** and maybe take a fifth.
Start planning a **small agency** run with AI.
Keep my half of the **rent** in savings.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **impatient** to build something.
S0.quote: I could run the whole office of a small care agency from my phone at the kitchen table.
fieldNote: She is a **self-employed** carer who already runs her business admin with AI.
Her ambition is a **small agency**, held back by her own inexperience.
The rented **family house** gives her a strong cushion.

steps.text: Keep four regular clients and take on a fifth
Draw up a plan for a small agency of three or four carers
Bank her half of the house rent each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for people who work for themselves. Small operators like me get the same office power as the big agencies. I'd say it with a bit of a grin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, it's perfect for me. The thinking AI does the matching, booking and invoicing, which is exactly what big agencies charge for. My hands-on work stays for years, because robots spread slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my small agency within the year, with two other carers to begin. I'd use AI for all the office work, so I'd keep costs low and pay my carers better than the big firms. I'd put some of my savings in to start it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big agencies' office staff, I suppose, and maybe the apps like CareBook, since families could book directly. The big agencies charge a third for an office that a phone can now run, and families will notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay carers better. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because good carers are hard to find, and I'd want them loyal. My mother always said look after your people and they look after you. It's also just good business.

Small operators get the same **office power** as big agencies.

My **hands-on** work stays for years while robots spread slowly.

S1.quote: The big agencies charge a third for an office that a phone can now run, and families will notice.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as a chance to **undercut** big agencies.
She frames paying carers well as both **family values** and good business.
She is ready to put her **own money** into the agency.

steps.text: Start a small care agency with two other carers
Run matching, booking and invoicing through AI tools
Put part of her savings into the new agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge change and people need to stand on their own feet. I wouldn't want the government taking over, but I'd want help for small businesses to buy robots. I'd tell the church to look after the older people who'll be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast for my plan. My carer income goes once robots arrive in 2031, and the big companies will have robots first because they've the money. I'd have three years to build an agency that then has to compete with robot firms. I don't know if that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the agency now anyway, but plan from day one to bring in robots when they come, maybe leasing them. I'd keep my clients personally until then. I'd keep the house as our safety, and Jonas and I would hold off on having a baby for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fired up as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on a baby. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, honestly. We wanted to start next year. My husband Jonas wants a baby next year, and I'd be asking him to wait while I race the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas's job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He fixes tractors and harvesters, and the robots would come for that too around 2031. But somebody fixes the robots, and he's good with machines. I'd tell him to start learning that side now.

say: I'd say people must **stand on their own** feet, without a government takeover.
I'd want help for **small businesses** to buy robots.
think: My carer **income** goes when robots arrive in **2031**.
Big firms get robots **first**, so three years may not be enough.
do: Start the **agency** now and plan to lease robots later.
Keep my own **clients** until robots arrive.
Hold off on a **baby** for a year or two.
S2.quote: My husband Jonas wants a baby next year, and I'd be asking him to wait while I race the robots.
fieldNote: She expects her own **carer income** to go and races to build a business.
The **baby decision** is where the speed costs her most.
She would bring in **robots** herself rather than fight them.

steps.text: Launch the care agency this year with two carers
Plan to lease care robots for the agency once they arrive
Put off trying for a baby with Jonas for a year or two
Keep seeing Mrs Lindqvist and Mr Barros herself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for people to get ready, so get on with it. I'd tell young people at church to learn a trade or start something. I'd be upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, it's tight but workable. I could build the agency for four or five years, make it known locally, then add robots around 2034. Thinking AI by 2031 only helps me, since I already use it for the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the agency in the next year, grow to five or six carers, and get good at the care myself. I'd learn about care robots as they come out and plan which ones to buy. Jonas and I would have our baby on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy about the big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would families pick your agency over a big robot firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'd know me from church and the school gate. Families will trust a local carer with a robot before they trust a robot sent from a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My carers, if I couldn't keep them all once robots came. I'd want to move them into checking on clients and doing the human bits. I'd feel responsible.

I'd tell young people at church to learn a **trade** or start something.
think: It's **tight but workable** to build the agency, then add robots around **2034**.
AGI in 2031 only **helps**, since I use AI for the office.
do: Start the **agency** next year and grow to five or six carers.
Study **care robots** as they come out.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a bit **uneasy** about big companies.
S3.quote: Families will trust a local carer with a robot before they trust a robot sent from a call centre.
fieldNote: She bets on **local trust** as her edge over big robot firms.
She already feels **responsible** for carers she hasn't hired yet.
Five years lets her keep her **family plans** unchanged.

steps.text: Start the agency next year and grow it to six carers
Follow new care robots and shortlist ones to buy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody has an excuse not to prepare. I'd tell people to build skills and savings. I'd be cheerful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. Ten years to build an agency, gain experience, and have a family. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven and running a business that uses robots, not one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the agency in a year or two, once I'm more confident with the care. I'd invest my savings in it slowly. We'd have our children and maybe buy a house with my half of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me getting comfortable. Or the government making rules that only big companies can follow. Ten years is plenty, unless the rules end up written so only the big care companies can afford the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents have thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad ran a bakery, so he'd understand. He'd say build it slowly and never borrow more than you can pay back. I still hear him every time I look at numbers.

fieldNote: Ten years removes her **time pressure** completely.

steps.text: Open the care agency within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to build an agency before robots arrive, and Jonas and I would have to delay a baby. What would help is fair access to robots for small businesses, and rules that don't only suit the big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who work for themselves. Nobody asks self-employed carers anything, because we don't have a manager to email the survey to.

She is traditional and entrepreneurial, and wants to start a **small agency**.
She is calm in the slow pictures and **anxious** in AGI by 2028, which forces a baby delay.
She plans to **bring in robots** herself rather than be replaced by them.
